content.value: Cloud computing is renting computers, storage, and services from a provider (like AWS, Google Cloud, Azure) over the internet instead of buying and maintaining your own physical hardware. Think of it like electricity — you don't build a power plant, you just plug in and pay for what you use.

content.title: Cloud Service Models
content.value:
graph TB
    subgraph SAAS ["SaaS (Software as a Service)"]
        S1["Gmail, Slack, Salesforce"]
        S2["You manage: Nothing"]
    end
    subgraph PAAS ["PaaS (Platform as a Service)"]
        P1["Heroku, AWS Elastic Beanstalk"]
        P2["You manage: App + Data"]
    end
    subgraph IAAS ["IaaS (Infrastructure as a Service)"]
        I1["AWS EC2, Google Compute Engine"]
        I2["You manage: App + Data + OS + Runtime"]
    end
    style SAAS fill:#1a2332,stroke:#10b981,color:#e2e8f0
    style PAAS fill:#1a2332,stroke:#f59e0b,color:#e2e8f0
    style IAAS fill:#1a2332,stroke:#ef4444,color:#e2e8f0

**IaaS** (Infrastructure) — You rent virtual machines and manage everything yourself. Maximum control. Example: AWS EC2.

**PaaS** (Platform) — You deploy your code, the platform handles the rest (OS, scaling, patches). Example: Heroku, AWS Elastic Beanstalk.

**SaaS** (Software) — You use finished software. No management needed. Example: Gmail, Slack.

AWS has 200+ services across 30+ global regions. You don't need to know all of them — focus on the top 10 that appear in 90% of interviews: EC2, S3, IAM, VPC, RDS, Lambda, CloudWatch, ELB, Route 53, ECS/EKS.

quiz.question: What type of cloud service is AWS EC2?
quiz.explanation: EC2 (Elastic Compute Cloud) is IaaS — you rent virtual machines and manage the OS, runtime, and applications yourself. AWS manages the physical hardware.

sections.title: EC2 — Virtual Machines in the Cloud

content.value: **EC2** (Elastic Compute Cloud) is AWS's virtual machine service. You can launch a server in seconds, choose the OS, configure the size (CPU, RAM), and pay only for the time it's running. Think of it as renting a computer by the hour.

content.title: EC2 Instance Lifecycle
content.value:
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Pending: Launch instance
    Pending --> Running: Instance ready
    Running --> Stopping: Stop instance
    Stopping --> Stopped: Instance stopped
    Stopped --> Pending: Start instance
    Running --> ShuttingDown: Terminate
    ShuttingDown --> Terminated: Instance deleted
    Terminated --> [*]

content.title: EC2 CLI Commands
content.value:
# Launch an EC2 instance
aws ec2 run-instances \
  --image-id ami-0c55b159cbfafe1f0 \
  --instance-type t3.micro \
  --key-name my-key \
  --security-group-ids sg-12345 \
  --subnet-id subnet-67890

# List running instances
aws ec2 describe-instances --filters "Name=instance-state-name,Values=running"

# SSH into your instance
ssh -i my-key.pem ec2-user@<public-ip>

# Stop / Start / Terminate
aws ec2 stop-instances --instance-ids i-1234567890abcdef0
aws ec2 start-instances --instance-ids i-1234567890abcdef0
aws ec2 terminate-instances --instance-ids i-1234567890abcdef0

content.title: EC2 Instance Types (Interview Must-Know)
content.value:
Family   Purpose              Example    Use Case
──────────────────────────────────────────────────────
t3       General purpose       t3.micro   Web servers, dev environments
m5       Balanced compute     m5.large   Application servers
c5       Compute optimized    c5.xlarge  Video encoding, ML training
r5       Memory optimized     r5.large   In-memory databases (Redis)
i3       Storage optimized    i3.large   Data warehousing, Elasticsearch
g4       GPU instances        g4dn.xl    Machine learning, rendering
t3.micro is in the AWS Free Tier — 750 hours/month for the first 12 months. Perfect for learning! Always use the smallest instance that meets your needs to save costs.

quiz.question: What is an EC2 instance?
options: A virtual machine (server) in the AWS cloud
quiz.explanation: EC2 is AWS's virtual machine service. An 'instance' is a single virtual server that you can configure with your choice of OS, CPU, RAM, and storage.

content.value: **S3** (Simple Storage Service) stores files (called 'objects') in containers (called 'buckets'). It's designed for 99.999999999% durability (11 nines!) — meaning if you store 10 million files, you'd statistically lose 1 file every 10,000 years. It's used for static websites, backups, data lakes, and media storage.

content.title: S3 CLI Commands
content.value:
# Create a bucket
aws s3 mb s3://my-company-assets-2024

# Upload a file
aws s3 cp backup.tar.gz s3://my-company-assets-2024/backups/

# Upload an entire directory
aws s3 sync ./public/ s3://my-company-assets-2024/website/

# List bucket contents
aws s3 ls s3://my-company-assets-2024/

# Download a file
aws s3 cp s3://my-company-assets-2024/backups/backup.tar.gz ./

# Delete a file
aws s3 rm s3://my-company-assets-2024/old-file.txt

# Make a bucket public (for static websites)
aws s3 website s3://my-company-assets-2024 --index-document index.html

content.title: S3 Storage Classes (Cost Optimization)
content.value:
Storage Class          Cost      Access            Use Case
───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
S3 Standard            $$$      Instant            Frequently accessed data
S3 Infrequent Access   $$       Instant            Monthly backups
S3 Glacier Instant     $        Instant            Archive with rare access
S3 Glacier Flexible    ¢        Minutes-12 hours   Long-term archival
S3 Glacier Deep        ¢¢       12-48 hours        Compliance archives (7+ years)

S3 bucket names are globally unique across ALL AWS accounts. Use a naming convention like: company-environment-purpose (e.g., 'opsacademy-prod-assets'). Never put sensitive data in publicly accessible buckets!

quiz.question: What does S3's '11 nines' durability mean?
options: S3 is available 99.999999999% of the time
If you store 10 million files, you'd lose 1 every 10,000 years
quiz.explanation: 99.999999999% durability means your data is extremely safe. S3 automatically replicates across multiple facilities, making data loss virtually impossible.

content.value: **IAM** controls WHO can do WHAT on WHICH resources in your AWS account. It's the security foundation — without proper IAM, a single compromised credential could wipe out your entire infrastructure.

    ROOT --> USER2["👤 User: bob\nDBA"]
    ROOT --> ROLE["🎭 Role: EC2-S3-Access\n(For services)"]

    USER2 --> GROUP2["👥 Group: DBAdmins"]
    GROUP1 --> POLICY1["📋 Policy: ReadWriteS3"]
    GROUP2 --> POLICY2["📋 Policy: FullRDSAccess"]

content.title: IAM Policy Example (JSON)

content.value: The #1 AWS security rule: NEVER use the root account for daily work. Create IAM users with minimum required permissions (Principle of Least Privilege). Enable MFA on the root account immediately.

quiz.question: What is the Principle of Least Privilege?
options: Give everyone admin access for convenience
Grant only the minimum permissions needed to perform a specific task
Use the root account for everything
quiz.explanation: Least Privilege means every user, service, and role should have only the permissions absolutely necessary for their job — nothing more. This minimizes damage if credentials are compromised.

content.value: A **VPC** is your own private network inside AWS. Think of it as building your own office complex in the cloud — you design the floor plan (subnets), install security doors (security groups), and decide which rooms have windows to the street (public subnets) vs. interior-only rooms (private subnets).

content.title: VPC Architecture
content.value:
graph TB
    IGW["🌐 Internet Gateway"] --> PUB1
    subgraph VPC ["VPC: 10.0.0.0/16"]
        subgraph PUB ["Public Subnet: 10.0.1.0/24"]
            PUB1["🌐 Load Balancer"]
            PUB2["🖥️ Bastion Host (SSH Jump)"]
        end
        subgraph PRIV ["Private Subnet: 10.0.2.0/24"]
            PRIV1["⚙️ App Servers"]
            PRIV2["🗄️ Database (RDS)"]
        end
    end
    PUB1 --> PRIV1
    PUB2 --> PRIV1
    PRIV1 --> PRIV2
    PRIV1 -->|"NAT Gateway"| IGW
    style VPC fill:#0f1923,stroke:#00d4ff33,color:#e2e8f0
    style PUB fill:#162231,stroke:#10b98133,color:#e2e8f0
    style PRIV fill:#162231,stroke:#ef444433,color:#e2e8f0

**Public Subnet** — Has a route to the Internet Gateway. Resources get public IPs. Used for load balancers and bastion hosts.

**Private Subnet** — No direct internet access. Used for application servers and databases. Can reach the internet through a NAT Gateway (outbound only).

**Security Groups** — Virtual firewalls attached to instances. Stateful: if you allow inbound traffic, the response is automatically allowed out.

**NACLs** — Network ACLs at the subnet level. Stateless: you must define both inbound and outbound rules.

Interview architecture: 'I'd place the load balancer in a public subnet, app servers in a private subnet, and the database in an isolated private subnet with no internet access. The app servers reach the internet through a NAT Gateway for pulling updates.'

quiz.question: Why put databases in a private subnet?
options: To prevent direct internet access — databases should only be reachable from app servers
quiz.explanation: Databases contain sensitive data and should never be directly accessible from the internet. Private subnets ensure only internal resources (like your app servers) can connect to the database.

content.value: AWS offers managed services that handle the heavy lifting of running infrastructure. **RDS** manages your databases. **Lambda** runs your code without any servers at all.

content.title: Managed vs Self-Managed
content.value:
graph LR
    subgraph SELF ["Self-Managed (EC2)"]
        A1["You manage EVERYTHING:\nOS patches, backups,\nscaling, monitoring,\nhigh availability"]
    end
    subgraph MANAGED ["Managed (RDS)"]
        B1["AWS manages:\nPatches, backups,\nreplicas, failover\nYou manage: Schema + queries"]
    end
    subgraph SERVERLESS ["Serverless (Lambda)"]
        C1["AWS manages:\nEVERYTHING\nYou manage: Just your code"]
    end
    style SELF fill:#1a2332,stroke:#ef4444,color:#e2e8f0
    style MANAGED fill:#1a2332,stroke:#f59e0b,color:#e2e8f0
    style SERVERLESS fill:#1a2332,stroke:#10b981,color:#e2e8f0

**RDS** (Relational Database Service) — Managed MySQL, PostgreSQL, MariaDB, Oracle, or SQL Server. AWS handles backups, patching, replication, and failover. You just connect and run queries.

**Lambda** — Serverless compute. Upload your function code, and AWS runs it in response to events (API calls, S3 uploads, scheduled tasks). You pay only for the milliseconds your code runs. Zero servers to manage.

content.title: Lambda CLI Example
content.value:
# Create a Lambda function
aws lambda create-function \
  --function-name process-order \
  --runtime nodejs18.x \
  --handler index.handler \
  --zip-file fileb://function.zip \
  --role arn:aws:iam::123456:role/lambda-role

# Invoke the function
aws lambda invoke --function-name process-order output.json

# View logs
aws logs tail /aws/lambda/process-order --follow
Lambda free tier: 1 million requests and 400,000 GB-seconds of compute per month — FREE forever. Perfect for microservices, API endpoints, image processing, and scheduled tasks.

quiz.question: What is AWS Lambda?
options: A serverless compute service that runs code without managing servers
quiz.explanation: Lambda is serverless — you upload code and AWS runs it in response to events. No servers to provision, scale, or maintain. You pay only for the compute time your code actually consumes.
